lines.text: From notches cut in a bone to the hum of the largest machine ever built, this is how people learned the laws of number and nature.
About twenty thousand years ago, someone in central Africa carved groups of notches into a baboon bone. It is among the oldest signs of people counting.
Around 1800 BCE, a Babylonian scribe pressed rows of numbers into clay that obey the rule of right triangles, a thousand years before Pythagoras.
In Egypt, a scroll of problems taught fractions, areas and the volumes of granaries. It is one of the oldest maths books we have.
Then came Pythagoras of Samos, who led a community in southern Italy devoted to number. The famous theorem about right triangles still carries his name.
Democritus made a bold guess: that everything is built from tiny particles too small to cut, moving through empty space. He called them atoms.
In Alexandria, Euclid gathered the geometry of his day and built it up from a handful of simple starting points.
His thirteen books, the Elements, proved each result step by step. Students would learn geometry from them for more than two thousand years.
In Syracuse, Archimedes worked out the lever, why things float, and how to measure curved shapes. He was killed when Roman soldiers took his city.
Centuries later, Hypatia taught mathematics and astronomy in Alexandria, until a mob killed her in 415 amid the city's bitter conflicts.
In India, Aryabhata gave a fine value for pi and explained day and night by the Earth spinning on its axis.
His successor Brahmagupta went further, writing the first rules for calculating with zero and with negative numbers.
With that, zero became a true number, and place-value counting could work. The idea travelled through the Islamic world and on to Europe.
Meanwhile the alchemist Jabir ibn Hayyan, known in Europe as Geber, described laboratory methods like distillation and crystallisation.
In Baghdad, al-Khwarizmi taught the Indian numerals and how to solve equations. Both the word algebra and the word algorithm come from him.
His book on equations, Al-Jabr, written around 820, gave the whole subject of algebra its name.
Ibn al-Haytham argued that we see because light enters the eye, and he tested his ideas by experiment, an early step toward the scientific method.
In 1202, Fibonacci's Liber Abaci brought the Hindu-Arabic digits to Europe, along with a puzzle about rabbits and a famous sequence of numbers.
Then Copernicus moved the Earth. He put the Sun at the centre, and his book appeared in the very year he died.
Galileo turned a telescope to the sky and saw the moons of Jupiter. For defending the Sun-centred picture, he ended his life under house arrest.
Kepler, working from Tycho Brahe's careful records, showed that planets travel in ellipses, not circles, and set out three laws of their motion.
In 1614, John Napier's logarithms turned multiplication into addition, speeding up the sums of astronomers and navigators for three centuries.
In France, the young Blaise Pascal built a calculating machine and, with Fermat, began the study of probability.
Robert Boyle linked the pressure and volume of a gas and insisted that ideas in chemistry be tested by experiment.
Around 1637, Pierre de Fermat scribbled in a margin that he had a proof of a simple-looking claim about powers. It would stay unproven for over three centuries.
That same year, Descartes joined algebra and geometry with coordinates, so that curves could be written as equations.
Isaac Newton found the laws of motion and universal gravity, split white light into colours, and helped invent calculus.
In Germany, Leibniz developed calculus at the same time, with much of the notation still used, and described the binary number system.
Back in 1654, letters between Pascal and Fermat about an unfinished game of dice had founded the mathematics of chance.
In 1661, Boyle's Sceptical Chymist attacked the ancient idea of four elements, a founding book of chemistry.
A few years later, Hennig Brand boiled urine hoping for gold and found phosphorus instead, the first element discovered by a known person.
By the 1680s, calculus was in print: the mathematics of change, of slopes and areas, which would come to underlie physics and engineering.
In 1687, Newton's Principia used mathematics to explain falling apples and orbiting planets with the same laws. Few books have mattered more.
In the next century, Leonhard Euler wrote on almost every corner of mathematics, gave us symbols like e, and kept working after he went blind.
Antoine Lavoisier showed that burning and breathing combine with oxygen, and that matter is never lost in a reaction. The Revolution sent him to the guillotine.
Alessandro Volta stacked metal discs into the first battery, giving science its first steady electric current. The volt is named for him.
In 1766, Henry Cavendish recognised hydrogen, the lightest element and the most common in the universe.
John Dalton proposed that each element has its own kind of atom with its own weight, and he described his own colour blindness.
In the 1770s, Scheele and Priestley found the gas we breathe, and Lavoisier named it oxygen.
Carl Friedrich Gauss transformed number theory and statistics, and became famous young for predicting the orbit of Ceres.
Humphry Davy used electricity to pull new metals, sodium and potassium, out of their compounds.
In 1789, Martin Klaproth found a heavy element called uranium. More than a century later it would fuel reactors and bombs.
That same year, Lavoisier's Elementary Treatise listed the known elements and laid the foundation of modern chemistry.
Michael Faraday, a bookbinder turned experimenter, showed that a moving magnet makes an electric current, the seed of electric power.
In 1800, Volta announced his pile of discs and wet cloth, and the electric battery was born.
A year later, Gauss, just twenty-one, published a book on number theory that founded the modern study of numbers.
Evariste Galois founded group theory as a teenager, then died in a duel at twenty.
George Boole turned logic into algebra. A century later, his true and false would run every digital circuit.
Bernhard Riemann imagined the geometry of curved space, a tool Einstein would one day need.
In 1828, Friedrich Wohler made urea, a substance of living things, from ordinary chemicals, and organic chemistry began.
James Clerk Maxwell joined electricity, magnetism and light into one theory, and showed that light itself is an electromagnetic wave.
Faraday's discovery of 1831, electromagnetic induction, is the principle behind every generator and transformer.
In Russia, Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the elements by weight and repeating properties, and boldly left gaps for ones not yet found.
Georg Cantor dared to count the infinite, founding set theory and showing that some infinities are bigger than others.
Nikola Tesla designed alternating-current motors and power systems that went on to light the world.
Max Planck found that light and heat are given off in tiny packets called quanta. With that idea, quantum theory began.
In 1859, Riemann made a guess about a pattern hidden in the prime numbers. It remains unproven, one of the great open problems.
In 1865, Maxwell's four equations described electric and magnetic fields, laying the ground for radio and modern electronics.
Two years later, Alfred Nobel invented dynamite. His fortune would fund the Nobel Prizes.
Marie Curie discovered polonium and radium with Pierre, coined the word radioactivity, and won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences.
In 1868, helium was found in the light of the Sun, before anyone found it on Earth.
A year later, Mendeleev's periodic table appeared, lining up elements of similar kind, its empty spaces waiting to be filled.
Ernest Rutherford, from New Zealand, showed that the atom has a tiny dense nucleus and that radioactivity turns one element into another.
Cantor's set theory, begun in the 1870s, became the common foundation on which most of mathematics is built.
Lise Meitner, who fled Nazi Germany, explained with her nephew Otto Frisch that a uranium nucleus could split, and named it fission.
Albert Einstein reshaped physics with relativity and the photoelectric effect, and his equation of mass and energy became the most famous in science.
Emmy Noether proved that every symmetry in physics goes with something conserved, like energy, and helped shape modern algebra.
Niels Bohr pictured electrons jumping between fixed levels, and his institute in Copenhagen became the home of quantum debate.
Erwin Schrodinger wrote the wave equation of the quantum world, and dreamed up a cat in a sealed box.
In India, Srinivasa Ramanujan taught himself mathematics and sent astonishing formulas to Cambridge, before dying young.
In 1895, Wilhelm Roentgen found rays that pass through flesh but not bone. Within months, doctors were using them.
A year later, Henri Becquerel saw that uranium gives off invisible rays of its own. Marie Curie named it radioactivity.
In 1897, J. J. Thomson showed that cathode rays are streams of tiny charged particles: electrons, the first piece of the atom.
In 1898, the Curies found radium, an element that glows in the dark.
At the turn of the century, David Hilbert set twenty-three problems that would guide mathematics for a hundred years.
Linus Pauling explained how atoms bond, and won two Nobel Prizes, one for chemistry and one for peace.
Enrico Fermi explained beta decay, then crossed to America, where he would build the first nuclear reactor.
Werner Heisenberg helped create quantum mechanics and found that some pairs of things can never both be known exactly.
John von Neumann worked on quantum theory, game theory and the design that most computers still follow.
J. Robert Oppenheimer would direct Los Alamos, where the first atomic bombs were built in the Second World War.
In 1904, Henri Poincare asked a deep question about three-dimensional shapes and spheres. It waited a century for an answer.
In 1905, Einstein showed that the speed of light is the same for everyone, and that moving clocks run slow.
From it came E equals m c squared: mass and energy are one and the same.
Kurt Godel, a logician from Austria, would show the limits of what mathematical proof can ever reach.
In 1907, Leo Baekeland made Bakelite, the first fully synthetic plastic, soon moulded into telephones and radios.
Two years later, the Haber process pulled nitrogen from the air to make fertiliser, helping to feed billions.
In 1911, Rutherford found that nearly all of an atom's mass sits in a tiny centre, the nucleus.
Alan Turing described an imagined machine that defined what computers can do, then helped break Enigma at Bletchley Park.
In 1913, Bohr's model set electrons in fixed orbits, explaining the light of hydrogen until quantum mechanics took over.
Francis Crick would help find the double helix of DNA, and later turned to the mystery of the brain.
Einstein's general relativity showed gravity as the bending of space and time, the key to black holes and the universe itself.
Richard Feynman shared a Nobel for quantum electrodynamics, drew his famous diagrams, and was a much-loved teacher.
Rosalind Franklin's X-ray photographs revealed the helical shape of DNA. She died of cancer at only thirty-seven.
By 1925, quantum mechanics had arrived: a theory of chance and tiny packets of energy that underlies chemistry, lasers and computers.
Two years on, Heisenberg's uncertainty principle said a particle's position and speed can never both be pinned down.
James Watson, with Crick, would propose the double helix and later lead the early Human Genome Project.
Peter Higgs would predict the particle that gives others their mass, and live to see it found.
In 1931, Godel proved that any consistent system of arithmetic holds truths it cannot prove, ending the dream of a complete mathematics.
In 1932, James Chadwick found the neutron, the uncharged particle in the nucleus.
In the thirties, Wallace Carothers' team at DuPont made nylon, first for toothbrushes and stockings, then for parachutes.
In 1936, the first Fields Medals were given, the highest honour for mathematicians under forty.
In 1938, Hahn and Strassmann split the uranium nucleus, and Meitner and Frisch explained the energy it released.
By 1941, Glenn Seaborg's team had made plutonium, element ninety-four, soon used in reactors and weapons.
On the second of December 1942, under a sports stand in Chicago, Fermi's reactor ran the first self-sustaining chain reaction.
In 1944, von Neumann and Morgenstern founded game theory, the mathematics of strategy.
In December 1947, Bell Labs built the first transistor, the tiny switch at the heart of every modern chip.
A year later, Claude Shannon founded information theory and defined the bit.
Born in 1953, Andrew Wiles would grow up to solve the puzzle that Fermat had left in his margin.
That same year, Watson and Crick, building on Franklin's images, showed DNA as a double helix, and how life copies itself became clear.
In 1954, Europe founded CERN near Geneva, a laboratory for the smallest particles, and later the birthplace of the Web.
In 1960, Theodore Maiman built the first laser, a narrow beam of one colour now used in surgery, scanning and fibre optics.
In 1964, physicists predicted the Higgs boson, the particle linked to how others get their mass. The hunt would take nearly fifty years.
Grigori Perelman would prove Poincare's conjecture, then turn down both the Fields Medal and a million-dollar prize.
Maryam Mirzakhani studied the geometry of curved surfaces and, in 2014, became the first woman to win the Fields Medal.
In 1991, Sony sold the first lithium-ion battery, the cell that now powers phones, laptops and electric cars.
In 1994, Wiles completed his proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, ending a hunt of more than three and a half centuries.
In 2002, scientists in Russia made oganesson, element one hundred and eighteen, completing the seventh row of the periodic table.
Two years later, Geim and Novoselov peeled graphene from graphite with sticky tape: carbon just one atom thick.
In 2008, the Large Hadron Collider switched on beneath France and Switzerland, and in 2012 it found the Higgs boson.
And in 2015, LIGO heard ripples in space and time from two colliding black holes, a century after Einstein predicted them.
From counting on a bone to hearing black holes collide, the questions keep leading somewhere new.
